newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta debt/interbank market closing report.
newsitem.headline: Peseta debt/interbank market closing report.

text.p: Spain's debt market erased initial gains, edging higher before the close on Monday, as dealers said trade activity was low, amid few new ideas.
"I am staying out, looking for a few clear opportunities. The mood here is 'wait and see'," a Madrid dealer said.
The long-bond future moved in between 116.06 and 116.44.
After a Reuter poll on Friday showed a slight majority in favour of a monetary easing at Tuesday's central bank repo, a few analysts have now changed their opinion.
"I changed my mind. My feeling now is that they would hold," said Jose Ramon Arechederra, trader at ABN Amro.
He said Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato's remarks on Friday, saying Spanish wage inflation was too high, suggested a cautious approach by the Bank of Spain.
"I can't imagine the Bank of Spain being more optimistic than a politician," he added.

The Bank of America in Madrid said in a note that despite the absence of international tensions that affected the last repo, recent data has nevertheless presented doubts about whether the Bank of Spain would cut. In particular, they referred to a rise in April industrial production and Q1 wage inflation.
"Industrial production shot up...prompting the question whether Spain's economy is suddenly accelerating in a way which would render further monetary easing unsustainable," it wrote.

"New focus on wage increases has strengthened the view that the failure to adjust rates on June 16 was a reflection of the Bank of Spain's concerns in this area and indeed a sign short term rates have bottomed in this cycle," they added.
But others were still of the opinion the bank could cut.
"I'm still thinking the Bank of Spain will cut its rate on Tuesday," Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid, said.
The 10-year spread over Bunds was a bit lower at the close trading at around 65 basis points, as dealers said it was likely to stay between 60 and 70 basis points all the week.
Trading activity was low, and also the yield curve was offering few opportunities, dealers said.
